The Ledger & Manual Journals

Merlin has no journal table. postings is a SQL view — a UNION ALL of one branch per posting source (sales invoice, purchase invoice, credit note, payment, manual journal) — read live from documents/document_lines. Every figure on the Income Statement, Balance Sheet, Trial Balance, and an individual account's transaction view is a query against this view. Nothing writes to it; there is nothing to keep in sync.

Why a view, not a table

An earlier version of Merlin posted to physical journal_entries/journal_lines tables at write time. That design was replaced: a written ledger and the documents it's derived from can drift apart if a write-time posting step is missed, skipped, or buggy for one document type but not another. A view has no such failure mode — a document appears in it (or doesn't) purely by virtue of its own current status and account columns, recomputed on every query. There is no posting step to forget to call.

How a document gets into the ledger

A document is "in the ledger" once its status is issued (see Document Lifecycle) and its accounts are configured — a sales invoice from sent onward, a purchase invoice from posted onward, a credit note from issued onward, a manual journal once posted. Each posting branch requires the relevant account column (receivable_account_id, payable_account_id, contra_account_id, tax_account_id) and, for invoices and credit notes, every line coded — one uncoded line hides the whole document from the ledger, not just that line, so a half-allocated invoice never shows a partial, misleading balance.

Account columns are stamped onto a document once, at the moment they're decided (e.g. when a sales invoice is sent), never read live from Settings at query time — a view has no portable way to join a settings table, and reading live would let a later Settings change retroactively re-post a historical document.

Balance by construction

Every invoice-type posting branch is balanced because the arithmetic behind it already is: accounts-receivable debit equals the invoice total, income credit equals the sum of line totals, and total = subtotal + tax_total is enforced whenever a document's totals are recalculated. There's no separate "does this balance" check for invoices, because there's nothing that could produce an imbalance.

A manual journal is different — its lines are written directly by a person, so nothing structural guarantees they balance. See Manual Journals below for how that's enforced instead.

Reversal is a new document, never an edit

Sales invoices can no longer be voided. The only way to reverse one is to issue a credit note against it — a new, independently posted document, dated in the period the mistake is discovered, not retroactively backdated into the period the invoice was issued. This keeps a closed period closed: a credit note issued in July for a March invoice leaves March's reports exactly as they were, and shows the correction in July where it belongs. See Quotes & Credit Notes.

Sum both sides Because a reversal is a second, independent posting rather than a mutation of the first, any report computing a signed total for an account must sum credit − debit (or the reverse for a debit-normal account) — never one side alone, or a credit note (or a reversing journal) has no visible effect.

Posted documents are immutable

Once a document is issued, its DocumentLine rows refuse to be saved or deleted — DocumentLine::saving()/deleting() throw PostedDocumentImmutableException. The document's own header columns that determine its ledger effect (total, subtotal, tax_total, issue_date, party_id, document_number) are frozen the same way. This is what makes the ledger's append-only guarantee real rather than aspirational: without it, editing an issued invoice's line or total would silently leave every report reading postings wrong, with nothing to notice.

The guard is bypassed only by saveQuietly(), used by a small number of trusted system paths that legitimately rewrite an issued document after the fact — foreign-exchange rate finalisation in DocumentService::recordPayment(), and every status/balance transition in DocumentService::transition() and applyCreditNote(). Each of those pairs its saveQuietly() call with a DocumentActivity row in the same transaction, so there's still a record of what happened even though Eloquent's own change-tracking was skipped — see Incident Notifications for how out-of-band changes (a direct database edit with neither) get detected.

Manual journals

A manual journal (Accounting › Journals) is a document like any other — document_type = 'journal' — for adjustments that don't belong to an invoice, payment, or credit note: accruals, depreciation, write-offs, corrections. Each line's amount is signed: a positive amount is a debit, a negative amount is a credit.

RuleEnforced by
A journal must balance — debits equal credits, to the centChecked before posting; a journal that doesn't balance can't be posted
A journal line can never post to an AR or AP control accountJournals adjust the general ledger directly; a customer or supplier balance is always changed through an invoice, credit note, or payment instead
A posted journal is permanentThe same header/line immutability guards as every other document type — see above

A draft journal can be edited freely — add, remove, or change lines, adjust the date and reference — until it's posted. Posting is a one-way step: there's no "un-post". If a posted journal turns out to be wrong, the correction is a new, sign-flipped journal (Reverse on the posted journal) dated in the period the mistake is discovered — the same reversal-not-edit principle as credit notes, applied to journals.

Because each journal line's own sign already says debit or credit, the postings view maps journal lines onto ledger rows one-to-one — unlike every other document type, which derives a fixed two-leg shape (e.g. one AR-debit row plus one income-credit row per line) from a single total. This is also why journals cost nothing on the reporting side: every report that reads postings picks up a posted journal automatically, with no journal-specific code of its own.

Bank statements never post

Uploading a bank statement never creates a ledger posting by itself — a statement exists purely for reconciliation. Each line is either matched against an existing document (a sales invoice being paid, a purchase invoice being settled) or, for something with no invoice behind it (bank charges, interest), turned into its own manual journal or GL-account posting on the spot. See Bank Statements.

Which reports read the ledger

Income Statement, Balance Sheet, Trial Balance, and an individual account's transaction view query postings directly — each collapses to a single grouped query.

Income by Account, Income by Client, Expenses by Account, and Expenses by Supplier deliberately still read documents/document_lines directly. Each needs data the view doesn't preserve at that granularity — an invoice count, the outstanding balance_due, or VAT split out per line rather than summed once per account across a whole invoice.

The balance_due formula

A related but separate concern: Document::recalculateBalance() is the single formula (total − amount_paid − credits_applied, floored at zero) that every writer of a document's balance_due must go through. applyCreditNote(), recordPayment(), and Document::recalculateTotals() all call it rather than assigning balance_due directly. credits_applied stores a credit note's amount uncapped — the same floor-at-zero in the formula handles a credit note larger than what remained owed, so nothing needs to clamp the credit itself.

status, amount_paid, balance_due, and credits_applied live on a separate document_balances table (one row per document), not on documents itself — that's the only part of a document that's ever mutable after creation. Model-level code ($doc->status, Document::create([...])) works exactly as before; a query-builder filter on one of these columns needs ->joinBalance() first.

A note on Eloquent date columns

A model attribute cast to 'date' is still stored as a full Y-m-d H:i:s value — Eloquent's fromDateTime() formats every date-typed cast using the connection's datetime format regardless of cast type. postings.entry_date is affected the same as every other date column in this app, so any query filtering on it uses whereDate(), never a raw where() comparison — the latter silently fails to match because of the stored value's trailing time component.
